title: Antibiotics, new medicines and monoclonal antibodies

steps.title: Antibiotics work on bacteria, and only bacteria
steps.body:
An **antibiotic** is a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them growing. It works because it **stops a process inside the bacterial cell that the host's cells do not have**, or do differently: building the bacterial cell wall, for example, or making proteins with the bacterium's own ribosomes. So the bacteria are harmed and the person's cells are not.

A **virus** has no processes of its own to stop. It reproduces inside the host's cells, using the host's machinery. An antibiotic cannot touch it without harming the cell, which is why doctors do not give antibiotics for a cold or flu.

Do not confuse the words: **antibodies** are made by your lymphocytes; **antibiotics** are drugs.

visuals.alt: A table comparing bacteria, viruses and human cells and whether antibiotics affect them

check.solution: **Chlamydia** is a bacterium. The others are viruses.

steps.title: Aseptic technique: growing only what you mean to
steps.body:
To test antibiotics in the lab, you first have to grow bacteria — and only the bacteria you want. **Aseptic technique** keeps other microorganisms out.

- **Sterilise** the growth medium (agar) and Petri dishes in an **autoclave**, which uses steam under high pressure to kill any microorganisms.
- **Flame the inoculating loop** until it glows red, then let it cool, so it carries only the bacteria you are transferring.
- **Keep dishes and culture vials covered**, lifting the lid only a little and only when needed, so microorganisms from the air cannot land on the agar.

In school labs the lid is also taped at two points rather than sealed, and cultures are grown at about 25 °C rather than body temperature, so harmful pathogens that thrive at 37 °C are less likely to grow.

nothing falls in from the air
Tape the lid, don't seal it

steps.title: Core practical: antiseptics, antibiotics or plant extracts
steps.body: This is Core Practical 5.18B. Bacteria are spread over an agar plate, discs soaked in different substances are placed on top, and after incubation each disc has a **clear zone** where the bacteria could not grow. The larger the clear zone, the better that substance is at stopping this bacterium.

steps.text: Using aseptic technique, spread bacteria evenly over a sterile agar plate
Soak paper discs of the same size in each substance, and one in **sterile water** as a control
steps.note: The control shows the paper alone does nothing

steps.text: Place the discs apart on the agar, tape the lid and incubate
Measure the diameter of each clear zone and work out its area
steps.note: Area, not diameter, is the fair comparison

steps.text: Independent variable: the substance. Dependent: the clear zone area. Control: disc size, volume, time, temperature, bacterium

check.prompt: In this practical, what is the dependent variable?
check.solution: You change the substance and **measure the clear zone**. Disc size and temperature are control variables.

markScheme.description: the area of the clear zone

options: the area of the clear zone
the type of substance on the disc
the size of the paper disc
the temperature of incubation

steps.title: Calculating areas with πr²
steps.body: Specification point 5.19B asks you to calculate the cross-sectional area of a bacterial culture, or of a clear zone, using **area = πr²**. You measure the **diameter** with a ruler, so the first step is always to **halve it**.

visuals.problem: A clear zone has a diameter of 14 mm. Find its area.

steps.text: Radius = diameter ÷ 2 = 14 ÷ 2 = **7 mm**
Area = πr² = π × 7²
= **153.9 mm²** (to 1 decimal place)

visuals.problem: A disc of diameter 6 mm sits in a clear zone of diameter 20 mm. Find the area of clear agar.

steps.text: Radii: 20 ÷ 2 = 10 mm and 6 ÷ 2 = 3 mm
Clear agar = zone − disc = π × 10² − π × 3²
steps.note: Take the disc away: bacteria were never under it

check.prompt: A culture has a diameter of 8 mm. Calculate its area. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
check.solution: r = 4 mm, so area = π × 16 = **50.3 mm²**.

steps.title: From discovery to medicine
steps.body:
Developing a new medicine, including a new antibiotic, takes many years and has several stages.

1. **Discovery**: a substance that might work is found, for example in a plant or a microorganism, or designed from knowledge of the disease.
2. **Development**: it is made in a form that can be tested, and its likely dose is worked out.
3. **Preclinical testing**: tested on **cells and tissues** in the lab, then on **animals**, to check it works and is not **toxic**.
4. **Clinical testing**: tested on **people**. First small doses on healthy volunteers, to check it is safe; then on patients, to find the best dose and whether it works.

In the best clinical trials some patients get a **placebo** — a dummy with no drug — and the trial is **double-blind**: neither patients nor doctors know who has which, so expectations cannot affect the results.

steps.title: Making monoclonal antibodies
steps.body:
A **monoclonal antibody** is one kind of antibody, made in large amounts, all identical, all complementary to the same antigen. The problem is that the lymphocytes which make a particular antibody **do not divide**, so you cannot grow many of them.

The answer is to combine two cells:
- a **lymphocyte** that makes the antibody you want (collected from a mouse given the antigen), which cannot divide;
- a **tumour cell**, which divides rapidly but makes no antibody.

Fused together they form a **hybridoma** cell. It divides again and again, and every copy makes the same antibody. That is where *monoclonal* comes from: antibodies from one clone of cells.

steps.text: A mouse is given the antigen, so it makes lymphocytes that produce the antibody
These lymphocytes make the right antibody but **cannot divide**
They are fused with **tumour cells**, which divide rapidly
The fused cell is a **hybridoma**
Hybridomas divide and make large amounts of identical antibody

check.prompt: What name is given to the cell made by fusing a lymphocyte with a tumour cell?

steps.title: What monoclonal antibodies are used for
steps.body:
Because each monoclonal antibody binds to **one specific antigen**, it can find one particular molecule or cell in the body.

- **Pregnancy tests.** Urine of a pregnant woman contains the hormone **hCG**. Antibodies complementary to hCG, on coloured beads, bind to it; antibodies fixed on the strip then hold it, giving a coloured line.
- **Diagnosis.** Antibodies carrying a radioactive or fluorescent marker bind to **blood clots** or **cancer cells**, so a scan shows where they are.
- **Treatment.** Antibodies carrying a drug or radioactive substance bind to **cancer cells** and deliver it there, or mark the cells for the immune system to destroy.

The advantage over ordinary drugs and radiotherapy is **targeting**: the antibody goes only to the cells with that antigen, so fewer healthy cells are harmed and there are fewer side effects.

visuals.alt: A table of the three uses of monoclonal antibodies, with what they bind to and what they do

check.prompt: Why can monoclonal antibodies cause fewer side effects than radiotherapy?
check.solution: They are **targeted**: they bind only to cells carrying the antigen, so healthy cells are largely left alone.
options: they bind only to cells with a specific antigen
they are cheaper to produce than other drugs
they are made by the patient's own body
they work more slowly than radiotherapy

steps.title: Your turn: compare two antibiotics
steps.body:
Two antibiotic discs on the same plate give clear zones of diameter 12 mm and 16 mm. Work out both areas before you look at the steps, then say by how much the larger one is bigger.

Notice that the diameters differ by a third, but the areas differ by much more. That is why the specification asks for areas: area grows with the **square** of the radius.

visuals.problem: Clear zones of diameter 12 mm and 16 mm

steps.text: Radii: 6 mm and 8 mm

steps.note: Nearly twice the area, from a third more diameter

steps.text: Conclusion: the 16 mm antibiotic is more effective against this bacterium

check.prompt: A clear zone has a diameter of 12 mm. Calculate its area. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
check.solution: r = 6 mm, so area = π × 36 = **113.1 mm²**.

steps.title: Going deeper: say what the drug does, and why it targets
steps.body:
The top marks in this topic go to answers that say **why**, not just **what**.

**Antibiotics.** Not *antibiotics kill bacteria* but *antibiotics stop a process in bacterial cells, such as making the cell wall, that human cells do not have*. Then the unfamiliar question — a new drug that blocks something — becomes easy: does the human cell have that thing?

**The core practical.** Compare **areas**, use a **control disc**, and conclude only about *this* bacterium.

**Monoclonal antibodies.** Say what each cell brings to the hybridoma: the lymphocyte the antibody, the tumour cell division. For uses, always come back to **specific binding**: that is what makes a pregnancy test work and what makes cancer treatment targeted.

**Trials.** Explain *why* double-blind: expectations cannot affect the results.

rows: stop a process bacteria have, host cells don't
larger clear zone area, against this bacterium
lymphocyte gives antibody, tumour cell division
binds only to cells with that antigen

check.prompt: A new drug stops bacteria making proteins with their ribosomes. Why could it still be safe for humans?
check.solution: Antibiotics must hit something that **differs** between bacterium and host. Human cells do make proteins, but their ribosomes are different, so a drug can block one and not the other.
options: human ribosomes are different from bacterial ones
human cells do not make any proteins
human cells have no ribosomes at all
human cells are protected by cell walls

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Antibiotics** stop processes in bacterial cells that host cells lack, so they only treat **bacterial** infections — never viruses.
- **Aseptic technique**: autoclave the agar and dishes; flame and cool the loop; keep lids and vials covered.
- **Core practical**: discs of each substance plus a sterile-water control on a lawn of bacteria; the bigger the **clear zone**, the more effective.
- **Area = πr²**: halve the diameter first; clear agar = zone − disc.
- **New medicines**: discovery → development → preclinical (cells, tissues, animals) → clinical (volunteers, then patients); placebos and double-blind trials.
- **Monoclonal antibodies**: lymphocyte (antibody, no division) + tumour cell (divides) → **hybridoma** → many identical antibodies.
- **Uses**: pregnancy tests (hCG), locating clots and cancer cells, targeted cancer treatment with fewer side effects.

visuals.alt: A summary table linking each idea to the key fact

questions.prompt: Name the piece of equipment used to sterilise agar and Petri dishes before use.
questions.solution: An **autoclave** heats them with steam under pressure, killing any microorganisms already there.

questions.prompt: In the core practical, what shows that a substance has stopped the bacteria growing?
questions.solution: Where the substance has stopped growth, there is a **clear zone** of agar with no bacteria around the disc. The bigger the clear zone, the more effective the substance.

Why can antibiotics not be used to treat viral infections?
questions.solution: Antibiotics work by stopping processes in **bacterial** cells. A virus has no processes of its own: it uses the host cell's, so an antibiotic cannot stop it without harming the cell.

questions.prompt: Why is an inoculating loop passed through a flame before it is used?
questions.solution: Heating the loop until it glows red **sterilises** it, so the only microorganisms transferred are the ones you mean to transfer. It is cooled before use so it does not kill them.
options: to kill any microorganisms on it
to warm the agar so bacteria grow
to make the loop easier to bend
to stop the lid from misting up

questions.prompt: A clear zone has a diameter of 14 mm. Calculate its area. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
questions.solution: Halve the diameter first: r = 7 mm. Area = π × 7² = π × 49 = **153.9 mm²**. Using the diameter instead of the radius is the most common mistake.

questions.prompt: Put the stages in developing a new medicine in order.
questions.solution: **Discovery** of a possible drug; **development** into a form that can be tested; **preclinical** testing on cells, tissues and animals; **clinical** testing on people.

markScheme.description: all four in the correct order

questions.prompt: In preclinical testing, what is a new drug tested on?
questions.solution: **Preclinical** means before people: the drug is tested on cells and tissues grown in the lab, then on animals, to check it works and is not toxic. People come next, in clinical testing.
options: cells, tissues and animals
healthy human volunteers
patients who have the disease
the scientists who made it

questions.prompt: Describe two aseptic techniques used when culturing bacteria, and explain why each is used.
questions.solution: Two techniques, each with its reason. Sterilise the agar and dishes in an autoclave, so no other microorganisms are already growing. Flame the inoculating loop, so it transfers only the intended bacteria. Keep the lid on the dish, so microorganisms from the air cannot get in.
questions.modelAnswer: The agar and Petri dishes are sterilised in an autoclave before use, so that no microorganisms are already present to contaminate the culture. The inoculating loop is heated in a flame until red hot and allowed to cool, so it transfers only the bacteria being studied. The lid is kept on the dish as much as possible, so microorganisms from the air cannot fall onto the agar.

questions.prompt: A paper disc of diameter 6 mm sits in the middle of a clear zone of diameter 20 mm. Calculate the area of clear agar, not counting the area under the disc. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
questions.solution: Clear agar = area of the zone − area of the disc = π × 10² − π × 3² = π × (100 − 9) = π × 91 = **285.9 mm²**. Both radii are half the diameters.

questions.prompt: Discs soaked in two antiseptics are placed on a plate of bacteria. The clear zone around A has a diameter of 18 mm; around B, 9 mm. A disc soaked in sterile water has no clear zone. What can be concluded?
questions.solution: A's clear zone is larger, so **A is more effective against this bacterium**. You cannot say *every* bacterium from one test, and B still has a clear zone, so it does have an effect. The water disc is the control: it shows the paper alone does nothing.

markScheme.description: A more effective than B against this bacterium

options: A is more effective than B at stopping this bacterium growing
A is twice as effective as B against every kind of bacterium
Sterile water is the best way to kill this kind of bacterium
B has no effect on the growth of this kind of bacterium at all

questions.prompt: Describe how you would investigate the effect of three different plant extracts on the growth of bacteria.
questions.solution: A plan with method, variables and aseptic technique. Sterile agar plate spread with bacteria; paper discs of the same size soaked in each extract, and one in sterile water as a control; lid taped on; incubate; measure the diameter of each clear zone and calculate the area with πr²; repeat and take means.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): some steps of a method
Level 2 (3 to 4): a workable method with some aseptic technique or control
Level 3 (5 to 6): a full method with aseptic technique, a control, variables and how to measure

criteria.text: A workable method: bacteria on agar, discs soaked in each extract
Aseptic technique and a control disc in sterile water
Measuring the clear zone, calculating area, and controlling variables

questions.modelAnswer: Using aseptic technique, spread bacteria evenly over a sterile agar plate with a sterile spreader. Soak paper discs of the same size in each of the three plant extracts, and a fourth disc in sterile water as a control. Place the discs on the agar, spaced apart, with sterile forceps. Tape the lid on, label the plate, and incubate it for the same time at the same temperature. Measure the diameter of the clear zone around each disc, halve it and calculate the area with πr². The larger the area, the more effective the extract. Keep the volume of extract, the disc size and the type of bacteria the same, and repeat the experiment to calculate a mean.

questions.prompt: Describe how monoclonal antibodies are produced.
questions.solution: Four stages: an animal is given the antigen, so lymphocytes that make the antibody are produced; those lymphocytes cannot divide, so they are fused with tumour cells, which divide rapidly; the result is a hybridoma cell; it divides and makes large amounts of identical antibody.

markScheme.description: lymphocytes that make the wanted antibody are collected
hybridomas divide and produce many identical antibodies

criteria.text: Lymphocytes that make the wanted antibody are collected
They are fused with tumour cells
Hybridomas divide and make large amounts of identical antibody

questions.modelAnswer: A mouse is injected with the antigen, so it makes lymphocytes that produce the antibody wanted. These lymphocytes make the right antibody but cannot divide. So they are fused with tumour cells, which divide rapidly but make no antibody. The fused cell is a hybridoma. It divides again and again, and every copy makes the same antibody, so large amounts of one identical antibody are produced.

questions.prompt: Why are lymphocytes fused with tumour cells to make monoclonal antibodies?
questions.solution: The lymphocyte brings the **antibody**; the tumour cell brings **rapid division**. Neither can do both, so the hybridoma combines them.

markScheme.description: lymphocytes make the antibody but cannot divide

options: the lymphocytes make the antibody but cannot divide
the tumour cells make the antibody but cannot divide
the lymphocytes divide but make the wrong antibody
the tumour cells kill any other bacteria present

questions.prompt: Explain how monoclonal antibodies can be used to treat cancer, and why this may cause fewer side effects than radiotherapy.
questions.solution: How: antibodies complementary to an antigen on cancer cells, carrying a drug or radioactive substance, bind only to cancer cells. Why fewer side effects: the treatment is delivered to those cells, so fewer healthy cells are damaged, whereas radiotherapy damages healthy cells in the area too.

markScheme.description: antibodies bind to an antigen found on cancer cells
they carry a drug or radioactive substance to the cells
so only cancer cells are targeted

criteria.text: Antibodies are complementary to an antigen on cancer cells
They carry a drug or radioactive substance to those cells
So the treatment reaches only the cancer cells
Whereas radiotherapy also harms nearby healthy cells

questions.modelAnswer: Monoclonal antibodies can be made that are complementary to an antigen found only on the cancer cells. A drug or radioactive substance is attached to the antibodies, so when they bind, the treatment is delivered straight to the cancer cells. Because the antibodies bind only to those cells, fewer healthy cells are damaged. Radiotherapy, by contrast, also damages the healthy cells around the tumour, which causes more side effects.

questions.prompt: In a double-blind clinical trial, neither the patients nor the doctors know who has the drug and who has a placebo. Why?
questions.solution: If a patient or doctor knew who had the real drug, their expectations could change how the patient feels or how results are recorded. Keeping both *blind* means any difference between the groups is due to the drug.

markScheme.description: so expectations cannot affect the results

options: So that expectations cannot affect the results
So that more patients agree to take part in it
So that the drug can be tested on more animals
So that the dose can be kept the same for all

questions.prompt: A new antibiotic kills bacteria by stopping them making cell walls. Why does it not harm human cells?
questions.solution: Antibiotics target a process the bacterium has and the host does not. **Human cells have no cell wall**, so a drug that blocks cell-wall making cannot affect them.

markScheme.description: human cells have no cell wall

options: human cells do not have cell walls
human cells make their walls much faster
human cells are too large for it to enter
human cells are protected by antibodies

questions.prompt: Explain how a pregnancy test uses monoclonal antibodies.
questions.solution: A pregnant woman's urine contains the hormone hCG. The test stick carries monoclonal antibodies complementary to hCG, attached to coloured beads. If hCG is present it binds, and fixed antibodies on the test strip hold the hCG and beads in place, giving a coloured line.

markScheme.description: urine of a pregnant woman contains the hormone hCG
monoclonal antibodies are complementary to hCG and bind to it
fixed antibodies hold it on the strip, giving a coloured line

criteria.text: A pregnant woman's urine contains the hormone hCG
Monoclonal antibodies complementary to hCG bind to it
Fixed antibodies on the strip hold it, so a coloured line appears

questions.modelAnswer: When a woman is pregnant, her urine contains the hormone hCG. The test stick contains monoclonal antibodies that are complementary to hCG, attached to coloured beads. If hCG is present, it binds to these antibodies. They move up the strip, where more antibodies fixed in the test window bind to the hCG and hold the beads in place, so a coloured line appears.

examTechnique.body:
This topic mixes three kinds of question: recall of aseptic technique and the stages of drug development; calculation, where πr² appears and the radius must come from the diameter; and application, where monoclonal antibodies or a new antibiotic are placed in a context you have not seen. The core practical can be asked as a method to describe, a table to interpret or a conclusion to judge.

For calculations, write the radius on its own line before anything else, and give area units as mm². For conclusions from clear zones, compare areas, refer to the control, and do not stretch a result on one bacterium into a claim about all of them. For monoclonal antibodies, every use comes back to one idea: they bind to one specific antigen.
examinerErrors: Using the diameter in πr² instead of halving it first.
Giving antibiotics for a viral infection, or writing *antibodies* when *antibiotics* is meant.
Describing an aseptic technique without saying why it is used.
Leaving out the control disc, or concluding about all bacteria from one plate.
Saying hybridomas are made from two lymphocytes, or not saying why a tumour cell is needed.
Mixing up preclinical and clinical testing: preclinical is cells, tissues and animals; clinical is people.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer explains that antibiotics work by stopping a process that bacterial cells have and host cells do not, and uses that to reason about unfamiliar drugs. It calculates areas cleanly, halving the diameter and subtracting the disc where needed, and draws conclusions from clear zones that are limited to the bacterium tested. It describes hybridoma production by saying what each cell contributes, and explains every use of monoclonal antibodies through specific binding, including why targeted treatment harms fewer healthy cells than radiotherapy.
